summary: Crew Health Navigator is a health monitoring app for astronauts on long missions, where the doctor on Earth is up to 20 minutes away and the crew medical officer is busy. Wearables and a 3-minute reaction test feed the data; the astronaut only reports how they feel. Every value is compared with that astronaut's own normal, learned with a Bayesian model, not with one limit for everyone. Each body system turns green, amber or red, every alert explains why, and the app says who should act: the astronaut, the medic on board, or the flight surgeon on Earth. A risk model with SHAP explanations flags problems early: in our simulated mission it warns about an infection two days before the fever. Real NASA blood tests of the Inspiration4 crew and NASA health standards ground the design.
details:
Crew Health Navigator watches the health of a five-person crew over a 30-day mission and tells each astronaut, in plain words, whether today is usual for them, why, and what to do next. It has three views. The crew mission view shows every astronaut's status, the risks for the next 48 hours and the day's tasks, which move to a fit crewmate when someone is unwell. The doctors' view gives the onboard crew medical officer a short "Right now" list and the flight surgeon on Earth a daily or weekly report. The check-in view shows one person: a clickable body map coloured by system, history charts with their usual range, and a medic tab for medicines and clinical notes.

How it works

Data arrives by itself. As on the space station, the wearable provides pulse, heart rate variability, blood pressure, sleep and exercise, and the 3-minute reaction test records reaction time. The astronaut only reports mood and symptoms. The crew medical officer logs medicines, writes notes in SOAP form and can type a reading by hand, only with a reason.

A personal norm. Each indicator starts from what is typical for people and is updated every day with the person's last 14 days (a Bayesian Normal-Inverse-Gamma model). Amber means outside the person's 99% band, or outside 95% two days in a row. Red is only for safety limits, each with a named source. One red reading asks to re-measure; only a confirmed red calls the flight surgeon, on a full screen that shows the signal delay.

Early warning with reasons. A random forest per event (infection, sleep disruption, deconditioning, low mood, CO2 exposure) gives the 48-hour risk as "times the usual level", recalibrated so the percentages can be trusted, and SHAP shows which signs raised it. When three or more crew members move the worrying way on the same day, the app points to a shared cause such as the air, noise or schedule.

Tomorrow's outlook. A second model, trained only on real people, forecasts a worse mood or less energy tomorrow.

Five places. The same crew can be moved to a Mars base, Moon base, space station, deep-space transit or Mars rover; each place has its own simulated mission with that place's hazards.

Results, on data the models never saw

The personal norm flags 93% of problems early, against 88% for a fixed median rule. The mood forecast scores 0.70 AUC on real people it never saw, against 0.61 for "same as today". The risk model warns as early as simple status rules but flags 38% of astronauts in a calm week instead of 73%, and reaches 0.94 ROC AUC for infection on 100 new simulated missions. We searched our own work for data leaks, found two and fixed them, so these are the honest numbers.

Benefits

Fewer false alarms for a busy medic, alerts that explain themselves, no step that depends on someone remembering, and only measured facts take a person off a task: a prediction just asks the medic to look. Everything runs offline, which matters with a 20-minute signal delay.

What we hope to achieve

Test the app with real wearables and an analog crew, start each personal norm from the astronaut's own pre-flight data, and review every limit and protocol with flight surgeons before any real use.

Honest limits

There is no open daily health data of astronauts. The crew and their 30 days are simulated, calibrated on real people, and labelled "synthetic" everywhere in the app. Good results on simulated missions show the approach works if early signs look like our simulation; they prove nothing about real astronauts. Not medical advice.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, SHAP; LightGBM for comparison; matplotlib for charts), FastAPI and Pydantic for the API, React, TypeScript, Vite and Recharts for the interface, pytest, ruff and ESLint for checks, Docker, and Render for hosting.

Our code: https://github.com/mat-satanism/CCKJAV-Health-Monitoring
